issues.legal_issue: Acceptance of payments after termination of a lease does not by itself create a new tenancy without the landlord’s assent to continued occupation.
material_facts: The tenant remained on the site after the lease had expired and the landlord had given notice terminating the lease.
The tenant sent payments equivalent to rent, but the landlord stated that the payments would be accepted under protest and applied toward compensation for use and occupation, not as rent.
The landlord had not agreed to the tenant’s continued occupation; the earlier eviction suit was withdrawn with liberty to bring a fresh suit.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s mere acceptance of payments after termination did not create a new tenancy or give the former tenant a right to remain in possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, a new tenancy requires the tenant’s continued possession as an offer and the landlord’s definite assent to it. Receipt of money alone is not conclusive; the parties’ intention and conduct must show assent. Waiver under Section 113 requires conduct showing an intention to treat the lease as subsisting and the other party’s consent. The Court relied on Raptakos Brett & Co. Ltd. v. Ganesh Property, Saleh Bros. v. K. Rajendran, Bhawanji Lakhamshi v. Himatlal Jamnadas Dani, R.V. Bhupal Prasad v. State of A.P., Karmani Industrial Bank Ltd. v. Province of Bengal, Konchada Ramamurty Subudhi v. Gopinath Naik, Kai Khushroo Bezonjee Capadia v. Bai Jerbai Hirjibhoy Warden, and Bhuneshwar Prasad v. United Commercial Bank.

rule.if: post_termination_tenancy_dispute and lease_term_ended and payments_accepted_after_termination and no_landlord_assent_to_continuance

predicates.post_termination_tenancy_dispute: The dispute concerns whether occupation continued as a tenancy after a lease ended.
predicates.lease_term_ended: The tenant’s contractual right to occupy had ended.
predicates.payments_accepted_after_termination: The landlord accepted payments from the former tenant after the lease ended.
predicates.no_landlord_assent_to_continuance: The landlord did not agree, expressly or by conduct, to the former tenant’s continued occupation as a tenant.

issues.definition: When a tenancy dispute concerns occupation after a lease has ended, and the landlord accepts payments but does not assent to continued occupation, the payments alone do not create a new tenancy.

issues.legal_issue: Rent-control protection for leased premises does not extend to a lease of vacant land merely because the tenant constructed structures on it.
material_facts: The lease was of a vacant site for use as a petrol outlet.
The lease allowed the tenant to construct accessory structures, and the showroom shed mentioned in the lease belonged to the tenant.
The landlord’s claim and notices described the premises as vacant land, and the landlord sought possession after removal of the tenant’s structures.
issues.conclusion: The lease was of vacant land rather than a building covered by the applicable rent-control statute, so the tenant could not claim statutory tenant protection under that statute.
issues.legal_principle: The Pondicherry Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1969 regulates the letting of buildings and defines a building to include a building or hut let separately for residential or non-residential purposes, along with specified appurtenances. A lease of vacant land on which the tenant may construct accessory structures is not, on these facts, a lease of a building under that definition.

rule.if: rent_control_protection_claim and lease_was_of_vacant_land and tenant_constructed_accessory_structures and structures_were_not_leased_from_landlord

predicates.rent_control_protection_claim: A tenant claims protection from eviction under a law regulating the letting of buildings.
predicates.lease_was_of_vacant_land: The property leased was vacant land rather than a building let by the landlord.
predicates.tenant_constructed_accessory_structures: The tenant constructed structures on the land for use connected with the leased activity.
predicates.structures_were_not_leased_from_landlord: The structures were not buildings belonging to the landlord that formed part of the premises let.

issues.definition: A claim to building-rent protection fails where the lease was of vacant land and the tenant, rather than the landlord, supplied the structures on it.

issues.legal_issue: A petroleum-storage licence requires a lawful right to the site, and continued occupation after termination of the lease does not itself preserve that right.
material_facts: The site had been occupied under a lease that expired, and the landlord declined to renew it and called for the tenant to surrender possession.
The tenant remained on the site, but the landlord had not assented to the continued occupation as a tenancy.
The tenant’s lease was of vacant land and did not attract the claimed statutory tenant protection.
The licensing authority’s licence related to the storage of petroleum at the site, and the tenant sought to retain or renew it despite the absence of a continuing lawful right to the land.
issues.conclusion: The phrase “right to the site” means a lawful right to continue on the land; mere or litigious possession is insufficient. Without such a right, the licensee cannot retain or renew the petroleum licence.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 153(1)(i) of the Petroleum Rules, 1976 provides for cancellation when the licensee ceases to have a right to the site for storing petroleum. That right is distinct from the permission to store petroleum on the site addressed by the no-objection-certificate provisions, including Rules 144 and 153(1)(ii). The Court relied on M.C. Chockalingam v. V. Manickavasagam, which held that juridical or litigious possession is not necessarily lawful possession, and on Bhawanji Lakhamshi v. Himatlal Jamnadas Dani and R.V. Bhupal Prasad v. State of A.P. concerning the effect of holding over without the landlord’s assent.

rule.if: petroleum_licence_site_right_dispute and lease_right_ended and landlord_refused_continuation and possession_only_after_termination

predicates.petroleum_licence_site_right_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a person may retain or renew a petroleum-storage licence for a particular site.
predicates.lease_right_ended: The lease that supplied the occupant’s right to use the site has ended.
predicates.landlord_refused_continuation: The landlord declined to renew the lease or otherwise assent to the occupant’s continued occupation.
predicates.possession_only_after_termination: The occupant relies on continued presence on the site, rather than a continuing legal entitlement, as the basis for claiming a right to the site.

issues.definition: Where a petroleum-licence dispute concerns a site whose lease has ended, and the landlord has refused continued occupation, possession alone does not preserve the licence without a lawful site right.

issues.legal_issue: A pending proceeding about a no-objection certificate does not prevent a court from considering a claim concerning the licensee’s right to the site.
material_facts: The landlord had separately approached the authorities seeking revocation of the no-objection certificate.
The landlord also sought a writ directing that the petroleum licence not be renewed, while the certificate-related proceeding remained pending.

The authority considering the no-objection certificate was concerned with the site’s location and suitability for petroleum storage, not ownership of the land or the legal nature of the applicant’s right to it.
issues.conclusion: The pending proceeding concerning revocation of the no-objection certificate did not bar the landlord’s writ proceeding or require the writ court to refrain from deciding the site-right issue.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 144 of the Petroleum Rules, 1976 concerns a no-objection certificate for the proposed site and does not require the authority to investigate ownership or the legal nature of the applicant’s right to the land. The Court distinguished that inquiry from the separate requirement under Rule 153(1)(i) that the licensee have a right to the site.

predicates.writ_proceeding_about_petroleum_licence: A writ proceeding seeks relief concerning the continuation or renewal of a petroleum-storage licence.
predicates.no_objection_certificate_review_pending: A separate administrative proceeding concerning a no-objection certificate for the site remains unresolved.
predicates.certificate_authority_considers_site_sui: The authority deciding the certificate issue assesses the site’s suitability rather than ownership or the applicant’s legal entitlement to the land.

issues.definition: A pending certificate review does not prevent a court from deciding a licence-related writ proceeding when the certificate authority’s inquiry concerns site suitability rather than land title.
